articles.title: How to read an instruction

body.support:
Instructions are short. But they matter a lot. Medicine boxes, sprays and signs all work the same way.

Most instructions have **three parts**.

1. **The action.** This is the doing word. It comes first. *Take. Keep. Shake. Do not.* It tells you what to do.
2. **The must-word.** *Must* means it is a rule. *Should* means it is good advice. *May* means it might happen. *May cause drowsiness* means it might make you sleepy.
3. **When and how.** Small bits like *with food* or *every 4 to 6 hours*. They tell you when and how. Don't skip them!

Medicine boxes have the **active ingredient** on the front. It is the part that makes the medicine work. Two boxes can have different names but the **same** active ingredient. Don't take both.

Signs are instructions too. *No diving. Shallow water.*

The big rule: **if you are not sure, ask.** A pharmacist will help you for free.
body.core:
Instructions are some of the shortest texts you'll ever read. They're also some of the most important. Medicine boxes, sprays, signs and chargers all use the same tricks.

Most instructions have **three parts**.

1. **The action.** This is the verb, and it usually comes first: *Take*, *Keep*, *Shake*, *Store*, *Do not*. It's a command. It tells you exactly what to do.
2. **The must-word.** Words like **must**, **should** and **may** show how strong the instruction is. *Must* (or *do not*) means it's a rule. *Should* means it's strong advice. *May* means something might happen: *May cause drowsiness* means it could make you sleepy.
3. **The when-and-how details.** Small phrases like *with food*, *every 4 to 6 hours*, *before bed* or *for up to 3 days* tell you when, how often and how. They're easy to skip, and they're often the part that keeps you safe.

Medicine boxes have one more thing to check: the **active ingredient**. That's the part that makes the medicine work, and it's printed on the front, near the name. Two boxes with different brand names can have the **same** active ingredient. Take both, and you've doubled the dose without meaning to.

Signs work the same way with fewer words. *No diving. Shallow water.* has an action (*no diving*) and a reason (*shallow water*).

The most important instruction isn't printed anywhere: **if you're not sure, ask.** You can ask a pharmacist about any medicine, and it doesn't cost anything.
body.extend:
Instructions are among the most compressed texts you'll ever read: a single line can carry a command, a limit and a warning. Medicine boxes, cleaning products, beach signs and manuals all use the same toolkit.

Most instructions have **three parts**.

1. **The action.** A verb in command form (an *imperative*), usually at the start: *Take*, *Store*, *Shake*, *Do not*. It makes the reader the one who acts.
2. **The must-word.** **Modal verbs** set the strength. *Must* and *must not* signal obligation: a rule. *Should* signals strong advice. *May*, *might* and *can* signal possibility: *May cause drowsiness* is a warning about what could happen, not a permission.
3. **The when-and-how details.** Phrases such as *with food*, *every 4 to 6 hours*, *before bed* or *for up to 3 days* add the circumstances: when, how often, how and how long. They're grammatically optional, which is why readers skip them, and practically essential.

Medicines add one more check: the **active ingredient**, the substance that makes the medicine work. Since 2020, Australian rules have required it to be easy to find on the front of the box. Different brands can share the same active ingredient, so reading only the brand name can lead to an accidental double dose.

Signs compress instructions further: *No diving. Shallow water.* gives a rule and its reason in four words.

The instruction that matters most isn't printed: **if you're not sure, ask.** Pharmacists answer medicine questions free of charge.

articles.vcNote: The three parts of an instruction: imperative verbs, modal verbs for obligation and possibility, and phrases giving circumstantial detail.

caseStudies.title: Why every medicine box changed

body.support:
In 2016, the **TGA** made new rules for medicine boxes. The TGA is the group that checks medicines in Australia. All boxes had to change by **2020**.

Why? To stop people making **mistakes** with medicines.

The big change was the **active ingredient**. Now it must be:

- on the **front** of the box
- under or next to the name
- in **bigger** writing.

Lots of medicines for pain, colds and flu have the same active ingredient. It is called **paracetamol**. The brand names are different. So check the active ingredient. Don't take two medicines with the same one.
body.core:
In 2016, the **TGA** brought in new rules for medicine labels. The TGA is the group that checks medicines in Australia. Companies had until **31 August 2020** to change their boxes.

The TGA wanted to cut down on **mistakes with medicines**. So labels had to be more alike, and the important parts had to be easier to see.

The biggest change was the **active ingredient**. Now it has to be:

- on the **front** of the box
- **below or next to** the name
- in **bigger** writing than before
- **easy to compare** with other boxes.

Why? Lots of medicines for pain, colds and flu have the same active ingredient: **paracetamol**. But they have different brand names. If you only read the brand name, you could take two with the same ingredient. The new labels make that easy to spot. But only if you look.
body.extend:
In 2016, Australia's medicines regulator, the **Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA)**, brought in new rules for medicine labels. Companies had four years to change their packs. The deadline was **31 August 2020**.

The TGA's goal was to **reduce medication errors**. Labels needed to be more consistent, and the key facts needed to stand out.

The biggest change was the **active ingredient**. It must now appear:

- on the **front** of the pack
- **below or next to** the medicine's name
- in **larger** text than before
- in a way that's **easy to compare** between products.

The reason is about how people really read. Many medicines for pain, fever, colds and flu contain the same active ingredient, **paracetamol**, under different brand names. A reader who only notices the brand could take two products with the same ingredient. Good design makes the key fact easier to find. But the reader still has to look.

caseStudies.title: Swim between the flags?

body.support:
Red and yellow flags on the beach mean: **swim between the flags.** That is where lifesavers are watching.

But a sign only works if people understand it.

In 2022, researchers from **UNSW Sydney** asked **249 people** about the flags. These people had moved to Australia from countries like India, Nepal and Afghanistan.

- **27%** did not know what the flags meant, or did not understand them well.
- Of the people who did know, **more than half** did not always swim between them.

The lead researcher said it is **“not their fault”**. Some people had never had swimming lessons. Some had trouble with English.

In many countries, **red means danger**. So the flags can seem to say the opposite!
body.core:
Red and yellow flags on an Australian beach mean: **lifesavers are watching this part. Swim between the flags.** Most Australians grow up knowing that. But a sign only works if everyone reads it the same way.

In 2022, researchers from **UNSW Sydney** surveyed **249 people**. They had all moved to Australia from countries such as India, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Afghanistan.

- **27%** didn't know about the flags, or didn't really understand them.
- Of the people who did know them, **54%** said they didn't always swim between them.

The lead researcher, Mark Woods, said it's **“not their fault”**. Some people had never had swimming lessons. Some found the English hard. The researchers said beach safety advice should be translated into people's own languages.

Other researchers point out that in many places, **red means danger**. So to someone born overseas, the flags can seem to say the opposite.
body.extend:
Red and yellow flags on an Australian beach mark **the area patrolled by lifesavers: swim between the flags.** For many Australians, that meaning is automatic. But a sign is a text. It only works if its readers share the code.

In 2022, **UNSW Sydney's Beach Safety Research Group** surveyed **249 migrants** from India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Afghanistan, Bhutan and Pakistan.

- **27%** did not know of the red and yellow flags, or did not have a good understanding of them.
- Of those who did know them, **54%** did not always swim between them.

The lead author, Mark Woods, stressed that it's **“not their fault”**. He pointed to barriers such as language and never having had swimming lessons. The researchers called for beach safety advice in people's first languages, and for more work with communities.

Other researchers have noted that in many countries, **red signals danger**. So a flag designed to mean *safe here* can read as *keep out*. The meaning of a symbol depends on the reader's background, not just the designer's plan.

teacher.overview: Students learn to read instructions closely: the imperative verb (the action), modal verbs that set the strength (must, should, may), and the phrases that give the circumstances (with food, every 4 to 6 hours). They apply this to a medicine label (finding the active ingredient), everyday product labels and safety signs, then write and test their own instructions. Two real cases: the TGA's medicine-label changes (active ingredients made easier to find) and a UNSW study showing many migrants misread the red and yellow beach flags.
prep: Collect a few **empty, clean** medicine boxes (pain relief, cold and flu) or print photos of them. Don't bring medicines into class; check your school's medication policy.
Optional: photos of real signs and labels from around the school (canteen, cleaning cupboard, pool, science lab).
Colour printing helps for the beach flags, or show them on screen.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Three parts
steps: **Hook (10 min):** put empty medicine boxes on desks. Race: find the active ingredient on each. Which two have the same one?
**Explicit teaching (10 min):** model the three parts (action, must-word, when & how) on one label, thinking aloud. Then do a second label together (guided).
**Watch (5 min):** explainer.
**Read (15 min):** article and Check your reading (independent).
**Exit (10 min):** one instruction from a box, split into its three parts.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Must, may and the detail
steps: **Explicit teaching (10 min):** must vs should vs may. Model the trap: *May cause drowsiness* is a warning, not permission.
**Sort (10 min):** Rule, advice or might happen?
**Annotate (15 min):** the medicine label (word bank for Foundation).
**Table (15 min):** The detail that matters; discuss what goes wrong when the detail is skipped.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Signs and real cases
steps: **Decode the sign (10 min).**
**Case study 1 (15 min):** why every medicine box changed. Link back to the active ingredient race.
**Case study 2 (20 min):** swim between the flags? Discuss: who is a sign written for? What happens when readers don't share the code?
**Exit (5 min):** one sign at school that could be clearer, and how.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Write it, test it
steps: **Model (5 min):** write two steps of a set of instructions badly, then fix them aloud.
**Plan + write (20 min):** final mission.
**Partner test (10 min):** the partner follows the instructions exactly as written, no questions. Where did they get stuck?
**Revise, Level Up, reflect (15 min):** fix one step, attempt the Level Up, quick check and request sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** examples — action: take, keep, shake, store, do not; must-word: must, should, may; when & how: with food, every 4 to 6 hours, before bed, for up to 3 days. Must = a rule; should = advice; may = it might happen. The active ingredient is what makes the medicine work; check it so you don't take two medicines with the same one. If you're not sure, ask.

**Sort:** 8 tablets — rule (do not); drowsiness — might happen (may); rest — advice (should); out of reach — rule (keep, a command); irritate eyes — might happen (can); skin test — advice (should).

**Label:** 1 active ingredient (paracetamol 500 mg); 2 uses (pain and fever); 3 directions: action *take*, dose *1 or 2 tablets*, how often *every 4 to 6 hours*, who *12 and over*; 4 limit, a rule (do not); 5 warnings: don't take other paracetamol medicines, keep from children; 6 emergency: call 13 11 26 straight away, even if you feel well.

**The detail that matters:** shake — *before use* (the medicine or product won't be mixed properly); sunscreen — *20 minutes before you go outside* (you could get burnt before it starts working); store — *below 25°C, away from sunlight* (it could spoil or stop working); fresh air — *only in a room with fresh air* (fumes could make you sick).

**Decode the sign:** slippery — *take care / walk carefully*; reason: the floor is slippery when wet. Do not mix — *don't mix it*; reason: mixing cleaning products can be dangerous. Flags — *swim between the flags*; reason: that's where lifesavers are watching.

**Case 1:** the TGA made the active ingredient easier to find (front, near the name, bigger, easy to compare) to reduce medication mistakes; different brands can share an active ingredient, so you could double up.

**Case 2:** swim between the flags (patrolled area). Some people didn't know the flags or hadn't had swimming lessons; language barriers; red can mean danger in other countries.

resources.label: UNSW — “It's not their fault”: beach flags study (2022)
Cancer Council — How to apply sunscreen

realityCheck: **No real medicines in class.** Use empty, clean boxes or photos, and check your school's medication policy. Never ask students to bring medicines from school or home; the case study question asks them to look at home with an adult.

**Some students already give medicine to others.** Many teens look after younger siblings or help a parent. Respect that knowledge, and keep the message to *read it, check it, ask a pharmacist*. The course uses adult (12 and over) directions on purpose; children's doses differ and come from the box or a pharmacist.

**Safe messaging.** The course is about everyday mistakes like doubling up, not overdose. In 2025 the TGA cut paracetamol pack sizes to reduce harm from intentional overdose; that's deliberately not used as a case study. If a student raises self-harm, follow your school's wellbeing process. Lifeline is 13 11 14 and Kids Helpline is 1800 55 1800.

**The beach case is about the sign, not the swimmers.** Some students may be recent arrivals or may not swim. Keep the focus on how a sign can fail its readers. Students who speak other languages are the experts here: ask how a sign would read to their family.
**The partner test is the bit students remember.** Following instructions exactly as written (no questions allowed) shows instantly where the writing is vague. Keep it light and fast.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's practical and low-tech, and the skills carry straight into Safety First at Work and L-Plate Ready.

levels.core: Standard version: three parts of an instruction, must/should/may sort, medicine label annotation, two detail tables, two real case studies, and a written and partner-tested set of instructions.
levels.extend: Adds exceed, persist and strength to the vocabulary, names the grammar (imperatives, modal verbs, circumstances), extra sort cards and table rows, and a Level Up on words with everyday and technical meanings.
